title: Mattress stitch seam
subtitle: An invisible join for flat crochet pieces worked side by side
excerpt: Mattress stitch seams two flat pieces together invisibly from the right side, by weaving between the edge posts of each piece in alternating passes. The seam is completely hidden once tightened. The technique is slower than whipstitch but the result is neater.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet — seaming methods. Standard British crochet and knitting finishing technique adapted for crochet fabric.

glossaryTerms.definition: A seaming method worked from the right side of the fabric, weaving between the edge bars of two pieces alternately. The seam is invisible once tightened, matching the fabric texture on both sides.
The horizontal bar visible at the edge of a crochet row — the strand connecting consecutive stitches along the side. Mattress stitch picks up these bars alternately on each piece.

heroPrompt: Two crochet panels in cream DK cotton laid edge to edge on a pale surface, with a tapestry needle mid-seam working mattress stitch between their edge bars — the seam nearly invisible from the front.

content.text: Mattress stitch seams the side edges of two flat pieces together while looking at the right side of both. A tapestry needle picks up the
on each piece alternately, creating a
that, when pulled snug, hides completely within the fabric. The right approach for side seams on jumpers, cardigan fronts and backs, and bag panels.
Lay both pieces side by side, right side up. Align the edges to be seamed.
Thread the tapestry needle with a length of matching yarn — about 1.5x the seam length.
Secure the yarn at the base of the seam by passing through the corner stitch of one piece, leaving a 10 cm tail.
Pass the needle under the edge bar of one row on the left piece (the horizontal strand between the last stitch and the one before it).
Pass the needle under the corresponding edge bar on the right piece, at the same row level.
Alternate: left piece, right piece, left piece, right piece. After every 4-6 rows, gently pull the seaming yarn taut. The pieces zip together, hiding the seam.
At the top of the seam, fasten off and weave in both the working end and the tail.
Keep the pick-up depth consistent — always one edge bar in from the edge, not two on some rows and one on others.
Tighten every 4-6 bars, not after every single stitch — tightening too often creates a puckered seam.
Use the same yarn as the project for an invisible join, or a contrast colour for a decorative visible seam (though whipstitch or slip-stitch seam look better as decorative seams).
